precepts.text: But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him. And Saul's servants said unto him, Behold now, an evil spirit from God troubleth thee. Let our lord now command thy servants, which are before thee, to seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.
precepts.point: So do not think just because you are here you may not be battling with that spirit right now. Just wait. You think the Lord wrote this in here for no reason? The Lord said if it had not been for the Lord, we would all be as Sodom. Now is that something where I am battling Sodom? No. The Lord said if it was not for the Lord we would all be as Sodom, all be in as destructive a state as Sodom and the cities of Gomorrah. We would all be worthy of that same destruction. So do not think, because you are not dealing with it right now, that spirit is going to tempt you at some point. The bitterness is going to tempt you. Hatred is going to tempt you. Unforgiveness is going to tempt you. Satan said, hold my cup.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

precepts.why:
Mark 7:22 names “an evil eye” among the evil things that come “from within, out of the heart of men”, and “All these evil things come from within, and defile the man.” 1 Samuel 18:9 says “Saul eyed David from that day and forward.” Was it with the looks of righteousness, or with an evil eye? An evil eye. And that evil eye defiled Saul even further, after the Lord had already rejected him. To see it, go back to where Saul’s trouble began, in chapter 16.

“But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” Saul was already battling some things. The Lord had rejected him, and an evil spirit from the Lord had taken him.

“And Saul’s servants said unto him, Behold now, an evil spirit from God troubleth thee. Let our lord now command thy servants, which are before thee, to seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.” They told him: find someone who plays cunningly on a harp, and that spirit will leave you.

There are building blocks of bitterness. Bitterness doesn’t just come about; there are other things first. Saul rejected the word of the Lord, and the Spirit of the Lord departed from him. That was the ground the evil eye grew in. And don’t think, because you are not battling that spirit right now, that it won’t come. Satan says, hold my cup. Wait until you get the new job offer, the promotion, the demotion, the transfer to another school or another city, where you are dealing with different spirits and different circumstances, and you wonder why you are being troubled in the spirit. If it had not been for the Lord, we would all be as Sodom.

precepts.text: And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him. So David did a good thing by playing the music to have that spirit depart from King Saul.
precepts.point: So do not think just because you are here you may not be battling with that spirit right now. Just wait. You think the Lord wrote this in here for no reason? The Lord said if it had not been for the Lord, we would all be as Sodom. Now is that something where I am battling Sodom? No. The Lord said if it was not for the Lord we would all be as Sodom, all be in as destructive a state as Sodom and the cities of Gomorrah. We would all be worthy of that same destruction. So do not think, because you are not dealing with it right now, that spirit is going to tempt you at some point. The bitterness is going to tempt you. Hatred is going to tempt you. Unforgiveness is going to tempt you. Satan said, hold my cup.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

precepts.why:
“And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.”

So David did a good thing by playing the music to have that spirit depart from King Saul. Saul did what the servants said, the spirit left him, and he was refreshed. He was like, man, I needed that. He was back in the spirit again. David was sent for Saul’s benefit, and Saul could not see it.

Now fast forward to chapter 18. Saul “eyed David from that day and forward”, and “it came to pass on the morrow, that the evil spirit from God came upon Saul.” The very next day after he had an evil eye towards David, meaning he was ready to do harm to David, that evil spirit returned. “And David played with his hand, as at other times: and there was a javelin in Saul’s hand.” David had already done this for him, as at other times. “And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it.”

That is how quickly hatred can progress: the man whose playing made the evil spirit depart becomes the target of the javelin. That is Mark 7: “an evil eye” comes from within and defiles the man. The evil eye brought the evil spirit back, and the bitterness turned into an attempt to kill.

precepts.text: Samuel anointed David in the midst of his brethren.
precepts.point: Even before the split, the men of Israel quarrelled with Judah over the king, saying, we have ten parts in the king. The words of Judah were fiercer, and the enmity stayed.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
David was anointed more than once, and it starts here in Bethlehem: “Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward.” Samuel anointed him in the midst of his brethren, and the Spirit of the Lord stayed on him from that day.

After Saul was dead, David went up to the cities of Hebron, and the men of Judah came and anointed David king over the house of Judah. So he was anointed again in Hebron, but only over Judah; he was the king of Judah in Hebron.

Then all the tribes came: “Then came all the tribes of Israel to David unto Hebron, and spake, saying, Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh.” They remembered that “when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel”, and that the Lord had said, “Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be a captain over Israel.” So “they anointed David king over Israel.” Now he is king over all twelve. “In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months: and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah”: both kingdoms. And “David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David.” Zion is the city of David.

But the beef was already there before the split. In 2 Samuel 19 the men of Israel asked, “Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away”; Judah answered, “Because the king is near of kin to us”: he is our tribe. Israel said, “We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more right in David than ye”: there are more of us than you, why can't we anoint him over here? “And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.” Judah cursed Ephraim out, and that enmity between the two stayed.

Ephraim felt more entitled, and in a way rightfully so: Joseph saved Israel from starvation in Egypt, Joshua of Ephraim brought us into the land and gave out the allotments, and Ephraim held Shiloh, Bethel and the first places of worship. So the anointing that began in the midst of David's brethren is also where the dividing hatred between Judah and Ephraim shows itself, a rivalry that went on long after David.

precepts.text: Samuel looked on Eliab and thought, surely the Lord's anointed is before him, but the Lord said, look not on his countenance or the height of his stature; man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. You short brothers can be great leaders.
precepts.point: Rich, poor, or middle class, none of it matters to the Most High; what man holds in high esteem, God calls abomination. The highest calling anyone can have on the face of the earth is to teach the word of God and compel the lost sheep of the house of Israel to come in, so do not think less of yourself because your name carries no prestige.

note.label: Judges 6: The Call of Gideon: Why Is All This Befallen Us

precepts.why:
When Samuel came to anoint a king, “he looked on Eliab, and said, Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him. But the Lord said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.”

The Lord did not look on Gideon's poor family or his place as the least in his father's house. He looked upon him and saw a mighty man of valour, and said, “Go in this thy might.” Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. You short brothers can be great leaders.

precepts.text: Men bear rule over sea and land, but yet the king is more mighty; this is the debate before the king of Persia over what is strongest.
precepts.point: The Most High told Samuel to go in with a heifer, as if coming only to sacrifice; he would go incognito, not letting it be known that he was coming to anoint Saul's replacement, and the Most High would show him whom to anoint.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“And Samuel said, How can I go? if Saul hear it, he will kill me.” Remember the influence and love Samuel had among the people; even so, this shows the power of the king. Saul raised no hand against Samuel yet, but a king had the authority to command a prophet’s death.

The debate before the king of Persia over what is strongest says the same: “O ye men, do not men excel in strength that bear rule over sea and land and all things in them? But yet the king is more mighty: for he is lord of all these things, and hath dominion over them; and whatsoever he commandeth them they do.”

precepts.text: The king is only one man, but if he command to kill, they kill; that is the power Saul held, and why Samuel had cause to be careful.
precepts.point: The Most High told Samuel to go in with a heifer, as if coming only to sacrifice; he would go incognito, not letting it be known that he was coming to anoint Saul's replacement, and the Most High would show him whom to anoint.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“And yet he is but one man: if he command to kill, they kill; if he command to spare, they spare”. The king is only one man, but if he command to kill, they kill. That is the power Saul held, and why Samuel had cause to be careful.

So the Most High told Samuel, “Take an heifer with thee, and say, I am come to sacrifice to the Lord.” He would go incognito, as if coming only to sacrifice, not letting it be known that he was coming to anoint Saul’s replacement, and the Most High would show him whom to anoint: “thou shalt anoint unto me him whom I name unto thee.”

precepts.text: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment; the same standard the Most High gave Samuel in this verse.
precepts.point: This still happens today: brothers will look at a group and assume the biggest one must be the leader, not knowing that brother might be the soldier while the leader is the slim one beside him.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
When Samuel looked on Eliab, he judged through his own lens as a man: “Surely the Lord’s anointed is before him.” The Most High corrected him: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him”. Looking the mightiest and the tallest does not make a man the one the Most High picked.

“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” That is the same standard the Most High gave Samuel in this verse: “man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.”

This still happens today. Brothers will look at a group and assume the biggest one must be the leader, not knowing that brother might be the soldier while the leader is the slim one beside him.

precepts.text: The rod out of the stem of Jesse is prophecy of Christ, out of this same lineage; the word repeated all through the verses is spirit, and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes nor reprove after the hearing of his ears.
precepts.point: This still happens today: brothers will look at a group and assume the biggest one must be the leader, not knowing that brother might be the soldier while the leader is the slim one beside him.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
The Lord told Samuel why he refused Eliab: “for the Lord seeth not as man seeth”. This scripture is heavy: it is showing the spirit of Christ before Christ walked the earth.

“And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots”. The rod out of the stem of Jesse is prophecy of Christ, out of this same lineage. The word repeated all through the verses is spirit: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord”. And “he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears”.

That is why the Pharisees could not understand why he dealt with the lower class instead of the mighty men. He was looking on the heart. He knew the Pharisees’ hearts were corrupt, while the humble were willing to devote their lives to the Most High.

precepts.text: We gave the fathers of our flesh reverence; how much rather should we be in subjection to the Father of spirits, for the Most High deals with the spirits of men, not the outside.
precepts.point: This still happens today: brothers will look at a group and assume the biggest one must be the leader, not knowing that brother might be the soldier while the leader is the slim one beside him.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“Furthermore we have had fathers of our flesh which corrected us, and we gave them reverence: shall we not much rather be in subjection unto the Father of spirits, and live?” The Most High is the Father of spirits. He deals with the spirits of men, not the outside.

That is why Eliab’s countenance and the height of his stature meant nothing: “the Lord looketh on the heart.”

precepts.text: In the context of selecting a leader over the congregation, the Most High is called the God of the spirits of all flesh; the selection is always spiritual.
precepts.point: This still happens today: brothers will look at a group and assume the biggest one must be the leader, not knowing that brother might be the soldier while the leader is the slim one beside him.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“Let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, set a man over the congregation, Which may go out before them, and which may go in before them, and which may lead them out, and which may bring them in; that the congregation of the Lord be not as sheep which have no shepherd.”

In the context of selecting a leader over the congregation, the Most High is called the God of the spirits of all flesh. The selection is always spiritual. So when Samuel came to anoint a king among Jesse’s sons, the Lord did not choose by countenance or stature; he looked on the heart.

precepts.text: I took thee from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel; from literal sheep to shepherd over the sheep of the house of Israel.
precepts.point: Taking a keeper of sheep and making him the shepherd of the nation is a pattern with the Most High; he took leaders and prophets from following literal flocks and set them to feed the flock of Israel.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, the older, bigger, more developed ones, and Samuel said, “The Lord hath not chosen these.” There remained “yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep.” Samuel would not sit down until he was fetched, and the Most High said, “Arise, anoint him: for this is he.”

The Lord sent word to David himself: “Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I took thee from the sheepcote, from following the sheep, to be ruler over my people, over Israel”. From literal sheep to shepherd over the sheep of the house of Israel. Taking a keeper of sheep and making him the shepherd of the nation is a pattern with the Most High.

precepts.text: He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds, from following the ewes great with young, to feed Jacob his people; sheep in the backyard to feeding the nation.
precepts.point: Taking a keeper of sheep and making him the shepherd of the nation is a pattern with the Most High; he took leaders and prophets from following literal flocks and set them to feed the flock of Israel.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds: From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.” Sheep in the backyard to feeding the nation.

The Most High took leaders and prophets from following literal flocks and set them to feed the flock of Israel. The youngest son who kept the sheep while his brothers passed before Samuel was brought to feed Jacob.

precepts.text: Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian, and led the flock to the mountain of God, where the Most High called him out of the midst of the bush.
precepts.point: Taking a keeper of sheep and making him the shepherd of the nation is a pattern with the Most High; he took leaders and prophets from following literal flocks and set them to feed the flock of Israel.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
David was not the first. “Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father in law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb.” There the Most High called him out of the midst of the bush.

Moses was following a literal flock when he was called, just as David was keeping his father’s sheep.

precepts.text: Moses was called from the flock of animals to bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt, and he ended up feeding them with the laws of the Most High.
precepts.point: Taking a keeper of sheep and making him the shepherd of the nation is a pattern with the Most High; he took leaders and prophets from following literal flocks and set them to feed the flock of Israel.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
At the bush the Most High said, “Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt.” Moses was called from the flock of animals to bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt, and he ended up feeding them with the laws of the Most High.

That is the same pattern as David: the keeper of a flock made the shepherd of the nation.

precepts.text: The Most High told Elijah to anoint Jehu to be king over Israel and Elisha the son of Shaphat to be prophet in his room.
precepts.point: The same pattern continues through the prophets: Elisha was taken from the plow and Amos from the herd.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
The same pattern continues through the prophets. The Most High told Elijah, “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel–meholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.”

As with Samuel at Jesse’s house, the prophet was sent to anoint the one the Most High named.

precepts.text: Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah cast his mantle upon him; he left the care of the literal flock, ministered to Elijah, and eventually became the prophet in his place.
precepts.point: The same pattern continues through the prophets: Elisha was taken from the plow and Amos from the herd.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
Elijah “found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.” Elisha was taken from the plow.

“And he left the oxen, and ran after Elijah”. He slew a yoke of oxen, “and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen, and gave unto the people, and they did eat. Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.” He left the care of the literal flock, ministered to Elijah, and eventually became the prophet in his place.

precepts.text: Amos was no prophet, neither a prophet's son, but an herdman and a gatherer of sycomore fruit, and the Lord took him as he followed the flock and said, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
precepts.point: The same pattern continues through the prophets: Elisha was taken from the plow and Amos from the herd.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
Amos was taken from the herd: “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and the Lord said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.”

The Lord took him as he followed the flock, as he took David from the sheep, and sent him to prophesy unto his people Israel.

precepts.text: The Lord raised up the holy spirit of a young youth named Daniel; another example of the spirit put on a man at a very young age.
precepts.point: David was also young when the spirit came on him, and that is nothing new either; the Most High does not choose the ones everybody expects, for the spirit of Christ was in the prophets he selected.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
David was young when the spirit came on him. He was the youngest son, and “the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward.” That is nothing new either.

“Therefore when she was led to be put to death, the Lord raised up the holy spirit of a young youth whose name was Daniel”. Another example of the spirit put on a man at a very young age. The Most High does not choose the ones everybody expects.

precepts.text: The spirit that was in the prophets when they were selected to feed the flock of Israel was the spirit of Christ, which testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ.
precepts.point: David was also young when the spirit came on him, and that is nothing new either; the Most High does not choose the ones everybody expects, for the spirit of Christ was in the prophets he selected.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come unto you: Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.”

The spirit that was in the prophets when they were selected to feed the flock of Israel was the spirit of Christ. So when “the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward”, it was the spirit of Christ in the one the Most High selected.

precepts.text: Not many mighty are called; the Most High did not choose the giants that were in the earth, he chose Israel, few in number; that is how he operates.
precepts.point: David was also young when the spirit came on him, and that is nothing new either; the Most High does not choose the ones everybody expects, for the spirit of Christ was in the prophets he selected.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty”.

Not many mighty are called. The Most High did not choose the giants that were in the earth; he chose Israel, few in number. He passed over Jesse’s older, bigger sons and chose the youngest, who kept the sheep. That is how he operates.

precepts.text: Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft; the road Saul took after the spirit departed ends with him literally at witchcraft.
precepts.point: Chapter 15 said rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and Saul is now headed down that downward spiral; the spirit is leaving him, and he will eventually become a reprobate and dabble in real witchcraft.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” Simultaneously, as the Most High put his spirit on David, the spirit departed from Saul. Note it well: the evil spirit came from the Lord. That is a teaching the church world leaves out.

Chapter 15 said, “For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.” Saul is now headed down that downward spiral. The spirit is leaving him, and the road Saul took ends with him literally at witchcraft: he will eventually become a reprobate and dabble in real witchcraft.

precepts.text: An evil man seeketh only rebellion, which is what Saul did in chapter 15, therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him; a cruel spirit sent to trouble him is what we see on Saul.
precepts.point: Chapter 15 said rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and Saul is now headed down that downward spiral; the spirit is leaving him, and he will eventually become a reprobate and dabble in real witchcraft.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why: “An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him.” Rebellion is what Saul sought in chapter 15, and now the cruel messenger is sent: “an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” A cruel spirit sent to trouble him is what we see on Saul.

precepts.text: Saul was tried by the laws of the Most High and went wrong; had he passed the test he would have been elevated, but wisdom forsook him and gave him over to his own ruin.
precepts.point: Why did the spirit leave Saul? Wisdom walks with a man by crooked ways at the first and tries him by her laws. Saul was put through a trial, whether he would keep the commandment given through the mouth of the prophet, and he went wrong; so the spirit forsook him and he was given over to his own ruin, that abyss of jealousy, envy, and hatred.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“Behold now, an evil spirit from God troubleth thee.” It was evident. Whatever Saul was doing and saying, his servants could tell an evil spirit was on him.

Why did the spirit leave Saul? Wisdom walks with a man by crooked ways at the first and tries him by her laws: “For at the first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him, and torment him with her discipline, until she may trust his soul, and try him by her laws. Then will she return the straight way unto him, and comfort him, and shew him her secrets. But if he go wrong, she will forsake him, and give him over to his own ruin.”

Saul was put through a trial, whether he would keep the commandment given through the mouth of the prophet, and he went wrong. Had he passed the test he would have been elevated, but wisdom forsook him and gave him over to his own ruin, that abyss of jealousy, envy and hatred.

precepts.text: Froward means contrary; Saul set his mind on the contrary of what the Most High commanded, and the holy spirit of discipline fled the deceit and would not dwell in a body subject unto sin.
precepts.point: Why did the spirit leave Saul? Wisdom walks with a man by crooked ways at the first and tries him by her laws. Saul was put through a trial, whether he would keep the commandment given through the mouth of the prophet, and he went wrong; so the spirit forsook him and he was given over to his own ruin, that abyss of jealousy, envy, and hatred.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
“For froward thoughts separate from God: and his power, when it is tried, reproveth the unwise.” Froward means contrary. Saul set his mind on the contrary of what the Most High commanded.

“For into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; nor dwell in the body that is subject unto sin. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and remove from thoughts that are without understanding, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in.” The holy spirit of discipline fled Saul’s deceit and would not dwell in a body subject unto sin, and his servants could see what came in its place: “an evil spirit from God”.

precepts.text: David and the captains of the host separated the sons of Asaph, of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals; musicians prophesying with instruments of music.
precepts.point: The songs we make and listen to, now that we know the truth, should be spiritual songs; the psalms were the jams of that day, and every one of them is deep, teaching who the daughter of Babylon is, the crafty counsel taken against us, and that the law was given to Israel.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
Saul’s servants proposed the remedy: “seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.” Our people understood back then that music is spiritual. The right playing could relieve an evil spirit.

“Moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals”. Musicians prophesying with instruments of music.

precepts.text: Teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord; the command is spiritual songs, sung to the Most High.

precepts.text: As the fat is taken from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.
precepts.point: David was also a singer; he praised the Most High with words of glory and sung songs with his whole heart, and he set up the singers before the altar, the same service we read of in 1 Chronicles 25.

“Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Beth–lehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the Lord is with him.” The servant did not say the name, but this son of Jesse who went hard on the instruments was David.

“As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.”

precepts.text: David sung songs with his whole heart and set singers before the altar to daily sing praises; praises in their songs, not filth.
precepts.point: David was also a singer; he praised the Most High with words of glory and sung songs with his whole heart, and he set up the singers before the altar, the same service we read of in 1 Chronicles 25.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
David was also a singer: “In all his works he praised the Holy One most high with words of glory; with his whole heart he sung songs, and loved him that made him. He set singers also before the altar, that by their voices they might make sweet melody, and daily sing praises in their songs.”

That is the same service we read of in 1 Chronicles 25, the singers set before the altar. Praises in their songs, not filth.

precepts.text: The king's favour is toward a wise servant; that is what David was as armourbearer. We know him as a mighty king, but he started out a wise servant, and that is how he got the king's favour.
precepts.point: Saul asked Jesse to let David stand before him, for he hath found favour in my sight; Saul liked the spirit on that young brother, and every king keeps a young soldier always with him.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

precepts.why:
Saul sent to Jesse, “Send me David thy son, which is with the sheep.” Jesse sent David with “an ass laden with bread, and a bottle of wine, and a kid”, and “David came to Saul, and stood before him: and he loved him greatly; and he became his armourbearer.”

These are David’s humble beginnings, serving at the king’s side. Even after the spirit had left Saul, David loved him and served him faithfully. Saul sent again, “Let David, I pray thee, stand before me; for he hath found favour in my sight.” Saul liked the spirit on that young brother, and every king keeps a young soldier always with him.

“The king’s favour is toward a wise servant: but his wrath is against him that causeth shame.” That is what David was as armourbearer. We know him as a mighty king, but he started out a wise servant, and that is how he got the king’s favour.

precepts.text: Young David was ruddy and of a beautiful countenance and goodly to look to, and the Most High said arise and anoint him, showing ruddy is a healthy youthful appearance.
precepts.point: His head is as the most fine gold, and his locks are bushy and black as a raven; this is the same as reading of the Christ having woolly hair and the Most High having hair of pure wool.

note.label: Song of Solomon 5: My Beloved Is White and Ruddy

precepts.why:
Ruddy is the same word used of young King David. “Now he was ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to. And the Lord said, Arise, anoint him: for this is he.”

Ruddy goes with a beautiful countenance and being goodly to look to: a healthy, youthful appearance with clean, clear, beautiful skin, not red. Samuel anointed him in the midst of his brethren, “and the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward.” That is what ruddy means of the beloved.

points: King David was chosen although King Saul was still in power.

Ruddy means no blemish. He was dark and lovely, just like that beauty product that they used to have in the stores. Dark and Lovely. That's what ruddy means; means black. And of a beautiful countenance: he was a handsome young man.

Samuel had groomed Saul up and saw potential in the brother, so he mourned over him; the Most High asked how long he would keep crying over the man he had rejected.
Samuel is told to fill his horn with oil and go to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for the Most High had already provided himself a king from among Jesse's sons.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

points: Samuel feared that Saul would kill him if he heard of it. Remember the influence and love Samuel had among the people; even so, this shows the power of the king. Saul raised no hand against Samuel yet, but a king had the authority to command a prophet's death.

The Most High told Samuel to go in with a heifer, as if coming only to sacrifice; he would go incognito, not letting it be known that he was coming to anoint Saul's replacement, and the Most High would show him whom to anoint.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

points: Samuel did what the Most High spake and came to Bethlehem, and the elders of the town trembled at his coming and asked, Comest thou peaceably? Everybody knew Samuel did not play; if he was coming to your town it was probably for some judgment.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

points: Samuel answered peaceably: he came to sacrifice to the Lord, and he sanctified Jesse and his sons and called them to the sacrifice.

note.label: 1 Samuel 16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart

The Most High corrected him: look not on his countenance or on the height of his stature, because I have refused him. Looking the mightiest and the tallest does not make a man the one the Most High picked.

The Lord seeth not as man seeth; man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. This scripture is heavy: it is showing the spirit of Christ before Christ walked the earth. The Pharisees could not understand why he dealt with the lower class instead of the mighty men; he was looking on the heart, and he knew the Pharisees' hearts were corrupt while the humble were willing to devote their lives to the Most High.
